title: Circular Buffer
description: Fixed-capacity ring buffer — writes past capacity overwrite the oldest slot. Modular arithmetic on head/tail indices keeps it O(1) per op.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the overflow policy and the API.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I'm building a fixed-size FIFO queue. write(v) adds to the back, read() pops from the front. Capacity is fixed at construction. The question is what happens when write is called on a full buffer — that's the policy decision."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• On write to a full buffer — overwrite the oldest (the ring-buffer / 'newest wins' policy), or throw / return false (the bounded-queue 'reject writes' policy)? Both are valid; pick one.
• What does read() on an empty buffer return — undefined, null, throw? I'd default to undefined.
• Do I need peek() (look at next-read without consuming), size(), isEmpty(), isFull()? Common follow-ups.
• Random access by index, or only sequential read/write?
• Single-threaded use, or do I need locking? JS is single-threaded so this is usually moot.
sections.why: The overflow policy is the load-bearing question because it changes the algorithm. Overwrite means tail advances on write when full (oldest gets dropped silently). Reject means write returns false / throws and tail doesn't move. Don't start coding until you've pinned this down — it's the kind of thing where the interviewer says 'oh I meant the other one' halfway through and you have to redo the write path. Saying 'I'll do the overwrite variant unless you'd prefer reject' shows you know both exist.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n)-per-op solution before discarding it.
sections.say:
"The brute force is: just use a plain array, push to the end, shift() from the front. shift is O(n) because every element has to move down one slot — that defeats the whole point of a queue. For an array-based queue you'd want push/shift or unshift/pop, and one of them is always O(n) on a contiguous array.

The insight: instead of moving elements, move POINTERS. Allocate a fixed-size array once. Keep two indices — head (next slot to write) and tail (next slot to read). On write, place at buf[head] then advance head with modulo. On read, take buf[tail] then advance tail with modulo. The elements never move; only the pointers do. That's O(1) per op.

The ring metaphor is exact — the buffer logically wraps around. When head reaches the end, modulo sends it back to 0. Same for tail. The two pointers chase each other around the ring."
sections.why: Naming 'move pointers, not elements' is the central insight — once you have that, the modulo arithmetic feels inevitable rather than arbitrary. The shift()-is-O(n) brute force is what most candidates implement first if they don't pause — calling it out shows you know why the ring approach exists. The 'pointers chase each other around the ring' image is the mental model that makes wrap-around feel intuitive.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern — API shape & invariant
sections.prompt: What's the data layout and what invariant disambiguates full from empty?
sections.say:
"The data layout is: `buf` — a fixed-size Array of length cap. `head` — next slot to write (0..cap-1). `tail` — next slot to read (0..cap-1). `size` — count of live elements (0..cap).

write(v): `buf[head] = v; head = (head + 1) % cap;`. Then check size: if it was already full, advance tail too (drop oldest); otherwise increment size.

read(): if size is 0, return undefined. Else `v = buf[tail]; tail = (tail + 1) % cap; size--; return v.`

The load-bearing invariant: `size` disambiguates the head === tail case. When head === tail, the buffer is either FULL or EMPTY — both states have the pointers in the same slot. Without a size counter, you can't tell which. Some implementations leave one slot always empty as a sentinel to use head !== tail as the discriminator, but the size counter is clearer and uses one fewer slot's worth of space.

The pattern is ring-buffer-mod. Same template powers every fixed-size FIFO queue: hardware ring buffers in OS kernels (network packet queues, keyboard buffers), audio buffers, the recent-N-items cache pattern, sliding windows over streams. Anywhere you want O(1) push-back / pop-front with bounded memory."
sections.why: The 'size disambiguates head === tail' insight is the question interviewers love — 'how do you tell full from empty?'. Having a one-sentence answer ('size counter, or sentinel slot, I'm using size for clarity') shows you've thought about it. Naming the sentinel-slot alternative unprompted is the senior move; it proves you know multiple implementations and have picked one for a reason. Connecting this to OS kernel ring buffers grounds the abstraction in a real use case.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few operation sequences to confirm the wrap-around behaves correctly.
sections.intro: "Let me trace a few sequences to confirm the pointers wrap correctly and the overwrite policy drops the right element." Each example shows `buf` slot-by-slot, head, tail, size, and collected reads. Three examples cover the canonical overwrite case (cap=3, four writes), the double-overwrite case (cap=3, five writes), and the interleaved write/read pattern.

examples.input: cap=3: write 1,2,3,4 → buf overwrites slot of 1; then 4 reads (last is undefined)
examples.note: Canonical overwrite case — fourth write hits a full buffer; head wraps back to slot 0 and tail also advances (dropping oldest=1). Then 4 reads consume 2,3,4 and the fourth returns undefined (size went to 0).
examples.trace:
init buf=[_,_,_] head=0 tail=0 size=0
write(1) → buf[0]=1, head=(0+1)%3=1, size 0->1, buf=[1,_,_]
write(2) → buf[1]=2, head=2, size 1->2, buf=[1,2,_]
write(3) → buf[2]=3, head=(2+1)%3=0 (WRAPS), size 2->3 (now FULL), buf=[1,2,3]
write(4) → buf[0]=4 (OVERWRITES the 1), head=(0+1)%3=1, FULL so tail=(0+1)%3=1 (drops oldest), size stays 3, buf=[4,2,3]
read() → buf[tail=1]=2, tail=(1+1)%3=2, size 3->2, return 2
read() → buf[tail=2]=3, tail=(2+1)%3=0, size 2->1, return 3
read() → buf[tail=0]=4, tail=(0+1)%3=1, size 1->0, return 4
read() → size===0 → return undefined
results = [2,3,4,undefined]

examples.input: cap=3: write 1,2,3,4,5 — TWO oldest dropped; reads yield [3,4,5]
examples.note: Double overwrite — fifth write past full means BOTH 1 and 2 get dropped. Tail advances twice during the overflow writes; reads then yield 3,4,5 in order.
examples.trace:
init buf=[_,_,_] head=0 tail=0 size=0
write(1) → buf=[1,_,_], head=1, size=1
write(2) → buf=[1,2,_], head=2, size=2
write(3) → buf=[1,2,3], head=0 (wrap), size=3 (FULL)
write(4) → buf=[4,2,3], head=1, FULL so tail=1 (drops 1), size stays 3
write(5) → buf=[4,5,3], head=2, FULL so tail=2 (drops 2), size stays 3
read() → buf[2]=3, tail=0, size=2, return 3
read() → buf[0]=4, tail=1, size=1, return 4
read() → buf[1]=5, tail=2, size=0, return 5
results = [3,4,5]

examples.input: cap=2 interleaved: write 1, write 2, read→1, write 3, read→2, read→3
examples.note: Interleaved write/read pattern with cap=2 — tail wraps from 1 back to 0 between the third write and the read; verifies the small-buffer wrap on both pointers. No overflow because reads keep up.
examples.trace:
init buf=[_,_] head=0 tail=0 size=0
write(1) → buf=[1,_], head=1, size=1
write(2) → buf=[1,2], head=0 (wrap), size=2 (FULL)
read()   → buf[0]=1, tail=1, size=1, return 1
write(3) → buf[head=0]=3 (overwrites slot 0 with 3), head=1, size 1->2 (NOT full anymore because we read, so we just increment size — no tail advance), buf=[3,2]
read()   → buf[tail=1]=2, tail=(1+1)%2=0, size=1, return 2
read()   → buf[0]=3, tail=1, size=0, return 3
results = [1,2,3]

sections.why: The first trace is the canonical sanity check — it confirms wrap-around AND the overwrite-drops-oldest rule in one pass. The second trace stress-tests the overwrite path by overflowing twice in a row, confirming tail advances every time on a full write (not just once). The third trace catches the subtle case where read() and write() interleave so the buffer never goes full — verifying that the size increment branch fires correctly and tail only advances on actual overflows.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Empty read → return undefined, do NOT advance tail or decrement size. The `if size === 0 return undefined` guard is what enforces this; without it, an empty read would advance tail past stale data and corrupt size.
• Full-then-pop sequence — write to capacity, then read read read. Each read frees a slot but tail wraps as it goes; head stays put. Confirms the size===0 guard fires at the right moment.
• Single-element buffer (cap=1) — every write overwrites the previous, head and tail are always 0. Degenerate but should still work; the modulo just keeps both indices at 0.
• Wrap boundary — head transitions from cap-1 back to 0. The `% cap` makes this transparent; without it, you'd index past the end of the array. Same for tail.
• cap=0 — degenerate / nonsensical. The buf array has length 0 so every write index is `0 % 0 = NaN` (or undefined behavior). Worth flagging that the constructor should probably reject cap<=0 with a throw.
• Concurrent producers/consumers — JS is single-threaded so this is moot, but in a real multi-threaded ring buffer you'd need a lock or atomic CAS on head/tail. Worth knowing it's the next layer of complexity.
• Storing undefined as a value — write(undefined) is indistinguishable from an empty slot if you don't track size separately. Another reason the explicit size counter is the cleaner design."
sections.why: The 'storing undefined' edge is the senior-candidate call-out — it's the bug that bites if you tried to infer size from buf entries instead of tracking it explicitly. Naming it defends the size counter as a design choice. The concurrent-producers/consumers edge is the kind of 'this would be much harder in C with threads' aside that shows you've thought about the abstraction beyond the JS happy path. The cap=0 edge is the cheap input-validation call-out that costs nothing to mention and shows you've thought about bounds.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time per op is O(1) — write does one assignment, one modulo, maybe one more modulo (on overflow). read does the same plus a guard. No loops, no scans, truly worst-case O(1) for every op.

Space is O(cap) — one fixed array, three scalar indices. No allocation after construction. This is actually the killer property: the buffer's memory footprint is bounded by cap regardless of how many writes it sees. That's why ring buffers are used in OS kernels and embedded systems where you can't afford a malloc on the hot path.

This is the ring-buffer-mod template. Same shape powers: OS kernel ring buffers (network packet queues, keyboard input buffer), DMA buffers, audio sample buffers, the LRU-cache-of-recent-N-items pattern, sliding windows over an infinite stream (sample the last N values). Anywhere 'fixed-size FIFO with O(1) push and pop' shows up.

The reject-on-full variant is one tweak away: on a full write, return false (or throw) instead of advancing tail. Same data structure, different overflow policy. Worth knowing both because some specs want one and some want the other."
sections.why: The 'bounded memory regardless of throughput' framing is the right defense of why anyone uses a ring buffer over a growable queue — it's the production-grade reason, not just an algorithmic curiosity. Naming OS kernel ring buffers as the canonical use case grounds the abstraction in something interviewers respect. The reject-on-full mention closes the loop on section 1's clarifying question — 'I picked overwrite, but here's the one-line change to reject'.

walkthrough.intro: Step through a sequence of CircularBuffer operations. Each example shows the underlying buf array (slot-by-slot), the head/tail pointers, the size counter, and the collected return values from every read(). Watch how writes past capacity advance tail too — that's the overwrite policy in action.

examples.label: cap=3: write 1,2,3,4 → buf overwrites slot of 1; then 4 reads (last is undefined)
cap=3: write 1,2,3,4,5 — TWO oldest dropped; reads yield [3,4,5]
cap=2 interleaved: write 1, write 2, read→1, write 3, read→2, read→3

trace: const snap = () => buf.map(x => x === undefined ? '_' : x);
yield { line: 8, label: `new CircularBuffer(${cap}) — buf=[${snap().join(',')}], head=0, tail=0, size=0`, state: { ops, cap, buf: snap(), head, tail, size, results: [...results] } };
yield { line: 11, label: `op#${k}: write(${op.arg}) — slot head=${head}`, state: { ops, cap, buf: snap(), head, tail, size, results: [...results], op: op.op, arg: op.arg } };
yield { line: 11, label: `buf[${head}] = ${op.arg} → buf=[${snap().join(',')}]`, state: { ops, cap, buf: snap(), head, tail, size, results: [...results], op: op.op, arg: op.arg } };
yield { line: 13, label: `head = (head + 1) % ${cap} → ${head}`, state: { ops, cap, buf: snap(), head, tail, size, results: [...results], op: op.op, arg: op.arg } };

yield { line: 16, label: `buffer was FULL — overwrite: tail advances ${oldTail} → ${tail} (oldest dropped, size stays ${size})`, state: { ops, cap, buf: snap(), head, tail, size, results: [...results], op: op.op, arg: op.arg } };
yield { line: 18, label: `not full — size++ → ${size}`, state: { ops, cap, buf: snap(), head, tail, size, results: [...results], op: op.op, arg: op.arg } };
yield { line: 22, label: `op#${k}: read() — size=${size}`, state: { ops, cap, buf: snap(), head, tail, size, results: [...results], op: op.op } };
yield { line: 22, label: `size === 0 → return undefined`, state: { ops, cap, buf: snap(), head, tail, size, results: [...results], op: op.op, got: 'undefined' } };
yield { line: 23, label: `read v = buf[${tail}] = ${v}`, state: { ops, cap, buf: snap(), head, tail, size, results: [...results], op: op.op, got: v } };
yield { line: 24, label: `tail = (tail + 1) % ${cap} → ${tail}`, state: { ops, cap, buf: snap(), head, tail, size, results: [...results], op: op.op, got: v } };
yield { line: 26, label: `size-- → ${size}, return ${v}`, state: { ops, cap, buf: snap(), head, tail, size, results: [...results], op: op.op, got: v } };

yield { line: 28, label: `all ops processed — collected results=${JSON.stringify(results)}`, state: { ops, cap, buf: snap(), head, tail, size, results: [...results], returns: JSON.stringify(results) } };

notes: Two indices (head=write, tail=read) plus a size counter — size disambiguates the full-vs-empty case where head === tail.
Decision: when full, additional writes overwrite the oldest element rather than throwing. Document the policy — both choices are valid.
All ops are O(1). Modulo on indices is the only trick — never reallocate.
Time O(1) per read/write. Space O(capacity).

questions.q: Why track `size` separately instead of inferring it from head and tail?
options: `(head - tail + cap) % cap` would be O(cap), not O(1)
When head === tail, it could mean either full or empty — size resolves the ambiguity
Modulo arithmetic on signed integers can produce negative values in JS
head and tail get reset to 0 between writes, so their difference is meaningless

questions.q: On a write to a full buffer (overwrite policy), which pointer must advance besides head?
options: Neither — head wrapping back to tail already overwrites the oldest
tail must also advance so the oldest entry is dropped
size must increment past cap so the overflow is recorded
tail must reset to head, since the read position is now invalid

questions.q: Time complexity of read() and write() on a circular buffer?
After capacity=3 and writes [1,2,3,4,5], what does the next read() return?

exercises.prompt: Complete the wrap-around logic so reads return the oldest surviving values after overwrites.

blanks.hint: increment size when not yet full

L3.prompt: Implement CircularBuffer(capacity) with write(v), read(), and a `size` field. Writes past capacity overwrite the oldest. With cap=3: write 1,2,3,4 then log size, read, read, read, read.
hints: Modulo on head and tail is the only wrap-around logic you need.
When full, advance tail on each write so the oldest element is the one discarded.
Reading an empty buffer should return undefined, not throw.
